name: Kingdom of Benin
summary: A West African kingdom ruled by the Oba from Edo (Benin City). It is famed for cast bronze and carved ivory art; many “Benin Bronzes” were looted by Britain in 1897.

knownFor.label: Benin Bronzes
knownFor.note: Thousands of cast brass plaques and heads; many were looted by Britain in 1897.

knownFor.label: Carved ivory
knownFor.note: Ivory tusks and masks, including the famous Queen Idia mask.

knownFor.label: Walls of Benin
knownFor.note: Huge earthen walls and moats around Benin City.

location.value: Southern Nigeria, centred on Edo (Benin City), with influence along the Niger delta and coast.
location.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

climate.value: Tropical, with a long rainy season.

resources.value: Palm oil, ivory, pepper, cloth and later slaves for trade.

urbanisation.value: Benin City was surrounded by vast earthen walls and moats, among the largest earthworks in the world.

economicBase.value: Yam farming, crafts and trade with Europeans from the 15th century.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Portugal from the 1480s, later with the Dutch and British.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowrie shells and brass manillas as currency.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

inequality.value: Wealth was concentrated in the Oba’s palace and among chiefs.

keyRulers.value: Eweka I (first Oba), Ewuare the Great (15th century), Esigie (early 16th century), Ovonramwen (1888–1897).

succession.value: Passed to the Oba’s eldest son (primogeniture).

institutions.value: Guilds of craftsmen (bronze casters, ivory carvers) and palace societies of chiefs.

stability.value: A long-lived monarchy for more than 700 years.

armyAndTech.value: Large armies; firearms acquired from Europeans.

majorWars.value: Wars of expansion under Ewuare; the British punitive expedition of 1897.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

territoryChange.value: Expanded under Ewuare and Esigie; annexed by Britain in 1897.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

alliancesRivals.value: Traded with Portugal; later conflict with Britain.

inventions.value: Lost-wax casting of brass and bronze.

openness.value: Traded with Europeans from the late 15th century, but controlled that trade.

religion.value: Edo religion with the sacred Oba at its centre; some Catholic influence from Portugal.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

languageWriting.value: Edo; no traditional writing, history kept in art and oral tradition.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

artsArchitecture.value: Cast brass plaques and heads, carved ivory, the walls of Benin City.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

socialStructure.value: The Oba, palace chiefs, town chiefs, guild craftsmen and farmers.

sharedIdentity.value: The Oba was seen as sacred.

neighbours.value: Yoruba states, Igala, Portugal and Britain.

colonisation.value: Annexed by Britain after the 1897 punitive expedition.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

peakPeriod.value: The 15th–16th centuries, under Ewuare and Esigie.

declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Benin (checked 6 Nov 2026); Plankensteiner (ed.), Benin Kings and Rituals (2007)

outcome.value: Annexed by Britain; the Oba still exists as a non-sovereign monarch in Nigeria.

sources.value: Oral traditions and European accounts. Checked against Wikipedia (“Kingdom of Benin”).
